title: RADAR: Redundancy-Aware Diffusion for Multi-Agent Communication Structure Generation
one_liner: Generate a task-specific communication graph for a multi-agent system step by step so that simple tasks use fewer links and hard tasks keep the links they truly need.
lead: This paper studies how agents in a multi-agent system should talk to each other. A fixed communication layout is often wasteful: easy tasks do not need everyone talking to everyone, while hard tasks may need a richer structure than the default one provides. RADAR treats the communication graph itself as something to generate. It builds the graph step by step, guided by a measure of how much each connection contributes, so that redundant links can be removed while useful coordination paths are preserved.

problem.h2: Why fixed communication layouts waste effort
paras: Multi-agent systems often assume one fixed pattern of communication. That is convenient, but it ignores the fact that tasks differ. Some tasks can be solved with only a few carefully chosen exchanges, while others need richer coordination.

Using too many links raises communication cost and can add noise because agents send messages that do not help. Using too few links can block useful cooperation. The paper asks whether the graph can be generated adaptively for each query.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Generate the communication graph progressively and favor links whose contribution justifies their cost for the current task.

panels.title: 1. Many agents are available
panels.viz_args: Specialists can exchange messages in many possible patterns
panels.caption: The number of possible communication graphs is large because many links can be turned on or off.

panels.title: 2. Fixed dense graph is wasteful
panels.viz_args: Everyone talks to everyone on an easy task
panels.caption: Dense communication wastes context space because many messages add no value.

panels.title: 3. Fixed sparse graph can miss help
panels.viz_args: A hard task lacks the needed coordination path
panels.caption: Too few links can hurt accuracy because useful specialists never exchange the right information.

panels.title: 4. RADAR grows the graph step by step
panels.viz_args: Add or keep links with clear contribution
panels.caption: The graph is generated progressively so that the final structure matches the task.

panels.title: 5. Better balance appears
panels.caption: The system improves task results while reducing unnecessary communication.

steps.text: Read the task and the available agents so that graph generation can be conditioned on what is being asked.
Produce the communication structure over several steps because one-shot graph choice makes fine adjustment difficult.
Use a redundancy-aware guide so that links that do not add useful coordination are less likely to survive.
Let agents communicate using the generated structure.
Check whether the new structure improves results while using fewer unnecessary messages so that the quality-cost tradeoff is visible.

paras: The paper changes the communication graph from a fixed design choice into a query-dependent object that can be generated and optimized.

hidden.name: Useful communication contribution of each link
paras: The key hidden quantity is whether a candidate link between two agents adds information that the task actually needs. A link can look harmless, but it may be redundant if the same information already arrives through another path.

RADAR estimates this hidden quantity while generating the graph. It favors links that increase effective coordination because those links improve the answer, and it discourages links that mostly repeat what other links already provide.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark links that are more likely to contribute unique coordination value for the current task.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether this communication link actually helps enough to be worth keeping because it adds information that other paths do not already provide.
The method generates communication topologies by estimating the effective contribution of links under a redundancy-aware objective.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: graph generation can remove repeated traffic while keeping the information paths that matter
paras: A fixed graph must choose one compromise for all tasks. That compromise is often poor because the best structure for a simple query is usually smaller than the best structure for a hard query. Step-by-step graph generation works better because it can grow or trim the structure to fit the current need.

The redundancy-aware guide is important because many links provide overlapping value. Penalizing repeated contribution helps reduce message volume, which improves efficiency because agents do not spend effort processing messages that do not change the final decision.

stages.s: Keep useful links, drop repeated ones

math.h2: Reward useful links and penalize redundant ones
math.words: A compact summary is to prefer a communication graph when it improves task success and preserves high-value coordination links, while subtracting a penalty for repeated or unnecessary communication.
math.equation: graph_score(G, q) = task_success(G, q) + useful_links(G, q) - redundancy_cost(G, q)
symbols: overall desirability of communication graph G for query q
how well the multi-agent system solves the task under graph G
benefit from links that add distinct coordination value for this query
penalty for links whose messages mostly repeat information already available elsewhere

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a planning agent needs tool results and a critic's check.
Graph A connects everyone to everyone. Task success 8, useful links 4, redundancy cost 7, total 5.
Graph B connects tool to planner, planner to coder, and coder to critic. Task success 8, useful links 7, redundancy cost 2, total 13.
Graph C keeps only planner to coder. Task success 4, useful links 3, redundancy cost 1, total 6.
Graph B wins because it keeps the links that matter while avoiding unnecessary traffic.

math.note: The paper uses conditional discrete graph diffusion with an effective-size guide rather than this exact formula, but the formula captures the tradeoff.

charts.title: Fixed or one-shot baselines
charts.note: The baselines either over-communicate or miss needed coordination because their graphs are not adapted carefully to each task.

charts.title: RADAR
charts.note: The paper reports better accuracy with lower communication cost across six benchmarks because the generated graph trims repeated links while preserving useful ones.

items.b: The generator may drop a rare but necessary link.
items.html: A link can look redundant in most cases yet be essential for one difficult query, so aggressive pruning can reduce task quality.
If graph generation itself is too expensive, some efficiency gains from reduced communication may be lost.
A rule learned on one benchmark may not transfer perfectly because the value of communication paths changes with agent roles and task structure.
The paper is useful because it treats communication design as an adaptive generation problem instead of a fixed architecture choice.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a four-agent system with distinct roles such as retriever, planner, coder, and critic. Give it tasks of varying difficulty. Compare three communication layouts: dense fixed, sparse fixed, and an adaptive graph generator that chooses links step by step.

The demo should log the generated graph, message count, and task result for every query. It should show that the adaptive layout keeps more links on hard tasks and fewer links on easy tasks because the value of communication changes with task complexity.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that generating the communication graph per query can improve the balance between coordination quality and message cost because easy tasks can use fewer links while hard tasks keep the ones they need.
